chunks: And Hammad narrated from al-Halabi, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), that he said:

Regarding a man who marries into a family, and his wife is 'awra' (has a defect) and they did not specify it to him, he said: 'The marriage is not annulled; rather, the marriage is annulled only from leprosy, leprosy-like skin disease, madness, and blindness.'

I asked: 'What do you think if he has consummated the marriage, what does he do with her dowry?' He said: 'She has the full dowry because he made her private part permissible to him, and her guardian who married her off is penalized with an amount equal to what he brought to her.'
Al-Sheikh (may Allah have mercy on him) said: 'And whenever the man is satisfied with one of those defects we mentioned, he has no right to annul it.'

key_terms.الْعَوْرَاءُ: The defective woman (one with a physical or mental defect)

ai.seo_question: What are the legal consequences if a wife's defect was concealed during marriage?
ai.summary: This hadith from Shaykh al-Tusi’s *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* clarifies that 'tadlis' (concealment) of specific defects like leprosy, madness, or blindness does not automatically void the marriage contract but grants the husband the option to annul it. If he chooses to retain his wife, she is entitled to the full dowry, while the guardian who concealed the defect bears financial liability. This ruling underscores the Shia jurisprudential principle that defects must be explicitly disclosed to be grounds for annulment, distinguishing between material defects and general satisfaction.
